name: Indoor tanning salon sessions

card.summary: Paying for timed UV bed or booth sessions to get a cosmetic tan, classed by the WHO's cancer agency as a carcinogen.
card.aka: Sunbeds, tanning beds, solariums, tanning booths
card.note: UV radiation is a Group 1 carcinogen per IARC; many jurisdictions restrict or ban commercial use, especially for minors.

quick.overview:
Indoor tanning salons rent time in UV tanning beds or standing booths that darken the skin without sun exposure. Customers are mostly motivated by appearance, since a tan is widely seen as signalling health, youth and attractiveness, and it is also used to prepare for holidays or avoid tan lines.

In looksmaxxing terms it belongs to the skin-colour and tan side of appearance work. Researchers who study the behaviour describe it largely through appearance motivation, and public health bodies treat it as a risk factor for skin cancer.
quick.mechanism: Lamps emit mostly UVA with a small share of UVB. UVA darkens melanin that is already in the skin, while UVB stimulates new melanin production, which gives a longer-lasting tan. Modern devices are described as producing little or no UVC.
quick.risks: The WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Meta-analyses have reported higher melanoma risk among ever-users, with higher estimates for those who began young. Reported harms also include burns, eye damage, photoaging and infection. Rules vary: Brazil and Australia ban commercial tanning, and many countries and US states prohibit use by under-18s.

lead: Indoor tanning salon sessions are timed uses of ultraviolet (UV) tanning beds or vertical booths, usually in a commercial salon, to produce a cosmetic tan. The devices use fluorescent or high-pressure lamps that emit mostly UVA with a small amount of UVB.[1]

Appearance is the most commonly reported reason for use. Surveys and psychology studies have examined appearance motivation, body-image factors and attitudes toward tanning as predictors of salon use, particularly among young people.[2][4][6] Other reasons reported include preparing for a holiday, avoiding tan lines and mood effects.[1]

UV radiation is classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as a Group 1 carcinogen. Meta-analyses summarised in encyclopedic sources report higher melanoma risk among people who have ever tanned indoors, with larger estimates for those who started at a young age.[1] Regulation varies widely, from bans on commercial tanning in Brazil and Australia to age restrictions in many other jurisdictions.[1]

paras: The most common device is the horizontal bed, also called a sunbed or solarium; vertical versions are called booths. Low-pressure beds typically run sessions of 15 to 20 minutes, high-pressure beds around 10 to 12 minutes, and booths 7 to 15 minutes.[1] Eye protection is required during use.[1]

In the US the Food and Drug Administration limits exposure times by the time needed to produce four minimal erythema doses, and the lamps are regulated as consumable parts separately from the beds.[1]

Danish physician Niels Finsen developed a UV carbon arc lamp in 1890 for treating skin disease and received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Tanned skin became fashionable in the 1920s, and early home sunlamps, which emitted a large share of UVB, tended to cause burns.[1]

German scientist Friedrich Wolff is credited with inventing the modern sunbed in 1975, using lamps that emitted about 95 percent UVA and 5 percent UVB. A salon opened in Berlin in 1977, and devices were sold in the US from 1978.[1]

Research on why people tan indoors has frequently applied psychological models. Studies using the theory of planned behaviour found that intentions and perceived behavioural control predicted salon use, and that appearance motivation and self-monitoring added predictive value in young people.[4][6] A prospective study using tripartite body-image theory examined appearance-based factors as predictors of both sunbathing and tanning salon use.[2] A 1993 survey also examined attitudes, beliefs and behaviour regarding tanning bed use, sunbathing and sunscreen.[3]

A 1992 survey of 220 adolescents in a US paediatric office found that most spent weekends in the sun while few always used sunscreen.[5] Encyclopedic sources add that most users are white women aged 16 to 25, and that users sometimes report mood improvement; industry claims that beds are more predictable than sunlight are contested by survey data in which more than half of indoor tanners reported burns.[1]

UV exposure damages DNA and is linked to basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.[1] A nested case-control study within the Nurses' Health Study examined constitutional factors and sun exposure in relation to all three cancer types.[7] A case-control study of basal cell carcinoma in young women examined the association with tanning bed use and smoking.[8]

Pooled analyses cited in encyclopedic sources report a 20 percent higher melanoma risk for ever-users, 59 percent for starting before age 35 in a 2012 analysis, and in a 2014 meta-analysis 16 percent overall and 35 percent for starting before age 25.[1] The same source summarises an estimate that indoor tanning accounts for more than 10,000 melanoma and about 450,000 non-melanoma cases a year in the US, Europe and Australia.[1]

Other reported effects include accelerated skin ageing, photokeratitis, ocular melanoma and bacterial contamination of equipment, as well as increased burn risk in people taking photosensitising medicines.[1] Excessive tanning that causes distress, sometimes called tanorexia, has been described as a form of dependence, and a 2017 Yale paper reported evidence of dependence.[1]

The industry has promoted vitamin D production as a benefit. Some researchers say moderate use can raise vitamin D levels, whereas most argue that the UVB doses exceed what is needed and that supplements and fortified foods are alternatives.[1] The US Federal Trade Commission has found it deceptive to market tanning for vitamin D without disclosing it is not necessary for production.[1]

France banned use by under-18s in 1997, and Brazil banned cosmetic tanning beds outright in 2009. Australia has banned commercial tanning services, and several EU countries, the UK and most Canadian provinces restrict minors.[1]

In the US the FDA raised tanning beds to moderate-risk devices in 2014 and requires a warning against use by under-18s, but there is no federal ban for minors. As of 2017, 15 states and DC banned under-18 use. A 10 percent federal excise tax was introduced in 2010.[1] A study of youth access laws questioned how well such laws operated in practice at tanning parlors.[9]

Estimates of US use vary: the FDA cited 30 million visitors a year in 2010 from industry data, while a 2015 JAMA Dermatology study found just under 10 million adults had tanned indoors in the prior year. CDC data show use among 18 to 29-year-olds fell from 11.3 percent in 2010 to 8.6 percent in 2013.[1] The number of US salons was estimated to have fallen from about 18,200 in 2008 to 12,200 in 2015.[1]

No intervention trials of tanning salon sessions as an appearance treatment were found. Research is observational or survey-based: case-control studies of skin cancer risk, and behavioural studies of why people tan.[7][8][4]

timeline.event: Niels Finsen develops a UV carbon arc lamp for skin therapy.[1]
Friedrich Wolff invents the UVA-dominant sunbed.[1]
A tanning salon opens in Berlin.[1]
France bans indoor tanning by under-18s.[1]
IARC classifies UV tanning devices and UV radiation as Group 1 carcinogens; Brazil bans cosmetic tanning beds.[1]
FDA reclassifies tanning beds as moderate-risk devices.[1]
Commercial tanning bed use is banned in Australia.[1]
